newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn retreats on gold, Bundesbank says no deal yet.
newsitem.headline: Bonn retreats on gold, Bundesbank says no deal yet.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl's government retreated on Tuesday from a controversial plan to revalue central bank gold reserves, but Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said a final deal had not yet been struck.

Finance Minister Theo Waigel, speaking after coalition deputies baulked at his unpopular grab for gold, told journalists he and Tietmeyer had reached "a good compromise" that would transfer windfall profits to Bonn only next year.
But Tietmeyer later said no deal had been reached and talks to resolve the unprecedented showdown were continuing.

German press commentators said even if the two sides reached agreement on the controversial revaluation plan, Waigel still had serious budget problems to tackle if Germany was to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

Waigel, desperately seeking 19 billion marks ($11 billion) to make up for 1997 revenue shortfalls, told Christian Democrat deputies in a closed-door meeting he had to cut spending and speed up privatisations to meet the Maastricht criteria.
"We will manage it in 1997," he told reporters afterwards.

Bundesbank council member Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher warned later on Tuesday however the country would not be able to reduce its budget deficit this year to 3.0 percent of gross domestic product, as required by Maastricht.

Bank analysts said the Bundesbank had won the unprecedented showdown and would now keep an eagle eye on Bonn to make sure it did not weaken the Maastricht criteria or agree with the new Socialist government in France to widen the first group of countries in the monetary union (EMU) in 1999.
"The Bundesbank is clearly the one that has come out on top of this," Ros Lifton, senior international economist at HSBC Markets in London.

The humbling climbdown appeared to end a six-day showdown between Kohl's hamstrung government and the Bundesbank, whose thundering rejection of any quick grab at its undervalued gold triggered a power struggle between Kohl and Tietmeyer.
But Tietmeyer muddied the waters later when he denied that a final agreeement had been reached.
"We have had only a talk, but of course no deal and the discussion is going on," he told reporters as he arrived in Interlaken for an International Monetary Conference meeting.
Waigel's drawn-out budget woes will continue regardless because he said he might still need to raise taxes, a move coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) vehemently oppose.

Pressure was also mounting within Kohl's own party as a group of regional CDU leaders criticised the beleaguered ruling coalition and said it should cut spending rather than raise taxes to fill gaping budget holes.
"The union should propose a consistent course of savings rather than talking about raising taxes," Christoph Boehr, CDU head in Rhineland-Palatinate, told the Rheinischen Post daily.
Criticism also poured down from press commentators.
"The Bonn coalition has not come one step towards solving its financial crisis," wrote the Frankfurter Allgemeine.
Die Welt daily said the government had its backs up against a wall, but said it had to push through the reforms Germany so desperately needed for economic recovery.
"We are in a difficult situation. It would be absurd (not to say so)," CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble said.

Waigel gave no details of the gold compromise but FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Otto Solms said only the Bundesbank's currency reserves would be revalued now, meaning Bonn would only benefit from the profits next year.
The gold deal as presented by the government appeared to emerge after Waigel and Tietmeyer met in Bonn.

The central bank was not in principle opposed to revaluing its gold reserves but insisted that the process should not take place until 1999, or at least not before the decision as to who will participate in monetary union, in May 1998.
The Bundesbank has some 95 million ounces of gold in its reserves, valued at 13.7 billion marks compared to a current market value of more than 55 billion marks.

The government's unprecedented grab for the gold raised eyebrows throughout Europe, especially in countries where German officials have long been delivering stern lectures against such budgetary sleight-of-hand.
Parliamentary deputies in Kohl's CDU and Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) pressed them to back down or face possible defeat in voting over the plan.
Michael Glos, head of the CSU parliamentary group, explained the retreat by saying differences between the Bundesbank and the government had been too small to fight over.
"A public dispute is not worth it either for the Bundesbank or for the government," he said. "We have a saying -- the smarter one backs down."
